html:
This is a working reference for the physics formulas that appear again and again in high school and first-year university courses: motion, forces, energy, rotation, gravity, fluids, waves, heat, electricity, magnetism, optics and modern physics.

Each of the 100 entries gives the formula, what every symbol means with its SI unit, when to use it, and a short worked example. Use it as a revision checklist. If you cannot say when a formula applies, or you cannot redo its example without looking, that is the one to practise.

How this was checked. Formulas follow the free OpenStax textbooks University Physics (Volumes 1–3) and College Physics 2e. Constants are the 2022 CODATA values published by NIST. Every worked example was recomputed in Python, and results are rounded to a sensible number of significant figures. Examples use g=9.8 m/s2g = 9.8\ \text{m/s}^2g=9.8 m/s2 unless stated otherwise. Full references are at the end.

Kinematics

The equations of motion for constant acceleration, plus projectiles (OpenStax University Physics Volume 1, chapters 3–4). In formulas 3 to 6, uuu is the initial velocity, vvv the final velocity, aaa the acceleration, ttt the time and sss the displacement.

1. Average speed and velocity

vˉ=ΔxΔt\bar{v} = \frac{\Delta x}{\Delta t}vˉ=ΔtΔx​

Symbols: Δx\Delta xΔx is displacement (m) for velocity, or total distance for speed; Δt\Delta tΔt is time taken (s).

Use it when: you need an average over a whole trip, not the value at one instant.

Example: A drive of 120 km in 1.5 h has an average speed of 80 km/h, or 80/3.6=22.280 / 3.6 = 22.280/3.6=22.2 m/s.

2. Acceleration

a=ΔvΔta = \frac{\Delta v}{\Delta t}a=ΔtΔv​

Symbols: Δv\Delta vΔv is change in velocity (m/s), Δt\Delta tΔt is time (s), aaa is in m/s².

Use it when: velocity changes at a steady rate, or you want the average acceleration.

Example: A car going from rest to 27 m/s in 9.0 s has a=27/9.0=3.0a = 27 / 9.0 = 3.0a=27/9.0=3.0 m/s².

3. Velocity–time equation

v=u+atv = u + atv=u+at

Use it when: acceleration is constant and you know (or want) the time, but not the displacement.

Example: A ball rolling at 5 m/s that accelerates at 2 m/s² for 4 s reaches v=5+2×4=13v = 5 + 2 \times 4 = 13v=5+2×4=13 m/s.

4. Displacement–time equation

s=ut+12at2s = ut + \tfrac{1}{2}at^2s=ut+21​at2

Use it when: you know the starting velocity, the acceleration and the time, and want the displacement.

Example: A stone dropped from rest falls s=12(9.8)(32)=44.1s = \tfrac{1}{2}(9.8)(3^2) = 44.1s=21​(9.8)(32)=44.1 m in 3 s.

5. Velocity–displacement equation

v2=u2+2asv^2 = u^2 + 2asv2=u2+2as

Use it when: time is unknown and not needed, such as braking-distance problems.

Example: A car at 25 m/s braking at 5 m/s² stops when 0=252−2(5)s0 = 25^2 - 2(5)s0=252−2(5)s, so s=62.5s = 62.5s=62.5 m.

6. Displacement from average velocity

s=(u+v)2 ts = \frac{(u + v)}{2}\,ts=2(u+v)​t

Use it when: acceleration is constant and you know both velocities and the time, but not the acceleration.

Example: A train speeding up from 10 m/s to 30 m/s in 20 s travels s=10+302×20=400s = \frac{10 + 30}{2} \times 20 = 400s=210+30​×20=400 m.

7. Range of a projectile

R=v02sin⁡2θgR = \frac{v_0^2 \sin 2\theta}{g}R=gv02​sin2θ​

Symbols: v0v_0v0​ is launch speed (m/s), θ\thetaθ is launch angle above horizontal, RRR is horizontal range (m).

Use it when: the projectile lands at the same height it was launched from and air resistance is negligible. Range is greatest at 45°.

Example: At 20 m/s and 45°, R=202×sin⁡90°/9.8=40.8R = 20^2 \times \sin 90° / 9.8 = 40.8R=202×sin90°/9.8=40.8 m.

8. Time of flight

T=2v0sin⁡θgT = \frac{2 v_0 \sin\theta}{g}T=g2v0​sinθ​

Use it when: the projectile lands at its launch height.

Example: At 20 m/s and 30°, T=2×20×0.5/9.8=2.04T = 2 \times 20 \times 0.5 / 9.8 = 2.04T=2×20×0.5/9.8=2.04 s.

9. Maximum height of a projectile

H=v02sin⁡2θ2gH = \frac{v_0^2 \sin^2\theta}{2g}H=2gv02​sin2θ​

Use it when: you need the peak height, where the vertical velocity is zero.

Example: At 20 m/s and 30°, H=400×0.25/19.6=5.10H = 400 \times 0.25 / 19.6 = 5.10H=400×0.25/19.6=5.10 m.

Forces and momentum

Newton's laws and the forces they act through (OpenStax University Physics Volume 1, chapters 5, 6 and 9).

10. Newton's second law

Fnet=maF_{\text{net}} = maFnet​=ma

Symbols: FnetF_{\text{net}}Fnet​ is net force (N), mmm is mass (kg), aaa is acceleration (m/s²). 1 N = 1 kg·m/s².

Use it when: relating the total force on an object to its acceleration. Always use the net force.

Example: A 1,200 kg car accelerating at 2.5 m/s² needs a net force of 1200×2.5=30001200 \times 2.5 = 30001200×2.5=3000 N.

11. Weight

W=mgW = mgW=mg

Use it when: finding the gravitational force on a mass. Mass stays the same everywhere; weight depends on ggg.

Example: A 60 kg person weighs 60×9.8=58860 \times 9.8 = 58860×9.8=588 N on Earth and 60×1.62=97.260 \times 1.62 = 97.260×1.62=97.2 N on the Moon.

12. Friction

fs≤μsN,fk=μkNf_s \le \mu_s N, \qquad f_k = \mu_k Nfs​≤μs​N,fk​=μk​N

Symbols: μs\mu_sμs​ and μk\mu_kμk​ are the coefficients of static and kinetic friction (no units), NNN is the normal force (N).

Use it when: surfaces are sliding (fkf_kfk​) or about to slide (maximum fsf_sfs​).

Example: Sliding a 50 kg box across a level floor with μk=0.30\mu_k = 0.30μk​=0.30 needs a force of 0.30×50×9.8=1470.30 \times 50 \times 9.8 = 1470.30×50×9.8=147 N to keep it moving at constant speed.

13. Hooke's law

F=−kxF = -kxF=−kx

Symbols: kkk is the spring constant (N/m), xxx is extension or compression from the natural length (m). The minus sign means the force opposes the displacement.

Use it when: a spring or elastic material is within its elastic limit.

Example: Stretching a spring with k=200k = 200k=200 N/m by 5.0 cm needs 200×0.050=10200 \times 0.050 = 10200×0.050=10 N.

14. Centripetal force

Fc=mv2r,ac=v2rF_c = \frac{mv^2}{r}, \qquad a_c = \frac{v^2}{r}Fc​=rmv2​,ac​=rv2​

Use it when: something moves in a circle. FcF_cFc​ is not a new force; it is the net inward force supplied by tension, friction, gravity or a normal force.

Example: A 1,000 kg car taking a 50 m radius curve at 15 m/s needs 1000×152/50=45001000 \times 15^2 / 50 = 45001000×152/50=4500 N of friction from the road.

15. Forces on an inclined plane

F∥=mgsin⁡θ,N=mgcos⁡θF_{\parallel} = mg\sin\theta, \qquad N = mg\cos\thetaF∥​=mgsinθ,N=mgcosθ

Use it when: an object rests or slides on a slope at angle θ\thetaθ, with no other forces perpendicular to the slope.

Example: For a 10 kg crate on a 30° slope, the force down the slope is 98sin⁡30°=4998 \sin 30° = 4998sin30°=49 N and the normal force is 98cos⁡30°=84.998\cos 30° = 84.998cos30°=84.9 N.

16. Pressure

P=FAP = \frac{F}{A}P=AF​

Symbols: PPP in pascals (1 Pa = 1 N/m²), FFF is force perpendicular to the surface (N), AAA is area (m²).

Use it when: a force is spread over an area.

Example: A 600 N person standing on 0.040 m² of shoe sole exerts 15,00015,00015,000 Pa. Balanced on a 1 cm² heel (10−410^{-4}10−4 m²), the pressure would be 6.0×1066.0 \times 10^66.0×106 Pa.

17. Momentum

p=mvp = mvp=mv

Use it when: analysing collisions, explosions and stopping forces. Momentum is a vector, in kg·m/s.

Example: A 0.145 kg baseball at 40 m/s has p=5.8p = 5.8p=5.8 kg·m/s.

18. Impulse–momentum theorem

J=F Δt=ΔpJ = F\,\Delta t = \Delta pJ=FΔt=Δp

Use it when: a force acts for a short time. Stretching the time reduces the average force for the same change in momentum.

Example: Catching that 5.8 kg·m/s baseball over 0.05 s takes an average force of 5.8/0.05=1165.8 / 0.05 = 1165.8/0.05=116 N. Stopping it in 0.005 s would take 1,160 N, which is why you pull your hands back when catching.

19. Conservation of momentum

m1u1+m2u2=m1v1+m2v2m_1 u_1 + m_2 u_2 = m_1 v_1 + m_2 v_2m1​u1​+m2​u2​=m1​v1​+m2​v2​

Use it when: no net external force acts during a collision or explosion. It applies to elastic and inelastic collisions.

Example: A 1,000 kg car at 20 m/s hits a stationary 1,500 kg car and they lock together: v=1000×202500=8.0v = \frac{1000 \times 20}{2500} = 8.0v=25001000×20​=8.0 m/s.

Work, energy and power

Energy accounting is often the fastest route to a mechanics answer (OpenStax University Physics Volume 1, chapters 7–8).

20. Work done by a constant force

W=Fdcos⁡θW = Fd\cos\thetaW=Fdcosθ

Symbols: FFF is force (N), ddd is displacement (m), θ\thetaθ is the angle between them. Work is in joules (J).

Use it when: a constant force moves an object. A force perpendicular to the motion does no work.

Example: Pulling a suitcase 20 m with 50 N at 30° above the horizontal does 50×20×cos⁡30°=86650 \times 20 \times \cos 30° = 86650×20×cos30°=866 J of work.

21. Kinetic energy

KE=12mv2KE = \tfrac{1}{2}mv^2KE=21​mv2

Use it when: finding the energy of motion. Doubling the speed quadruples the kinetic energy.

Example: A 1,000 kg car at 20 m/s has 12(1000)(202)=200,000\tfrac{1}{2}(1000)(20^2) = 200{,}00021​(1000)(202)=200,000 J, or 200 kJ.

22. Gravitational potential energy (near Earth)

PE=mghPE = mghPE=mgh

Use it when: height changes are small compared with Earth's radius. For orbits, use formula 41.

Example: A 70 kg person climbing 3.0 m of stairs gains 70×9.8×3.0=205870 \times 9.8 \times 3.0 = 205870×9.8×3.0=2058 J, about 2.1 kJ.

23. Elastic potential energy

PEspring=12kx2PE_{\text{spring}} = \tfrac{1}{2}kx^2PEspring​=21​kx2

Use it when: energy is stored in a stretched or compressed spring.

Example: A spring with k=400k = 400k=400 N/m compressed by 0.10 m stores 12(400)(0.102)=2.0\tfrac{1}{2}(400)(0.10^2) = 2.021​(400)(0.102)=2.0 J.

24. Work–energy theorem

Wnet=ΔKE=12mv2−12mu2W_{\text{net}} = \Delta KE = \tfrac{1}{2}mv^2 - \tfrac{1}{2}mu^2Wnet​=ΔKE=21​mv2−21​mu2

Use it when: you know the net work and want a speed, or the other way round, without needing time.

Example: Slowing a 1,000 kg car from 20 m/s to 10 m/s takes W=50,000−200,000=−150,000W = 50{,}000 - 200{,}000 = -150{,}000W=50,000−200,000=−150,000 J. The negative sign means the brakes remove energy.

25. Power

P=Wt=ΔEtP = \frac{W}{t} = \frac{\Delta E}{t}P=tW​=tΔE​

Use it when: you need the rate of energy transfer. Power is in watts (1 W = 1 J/s).

Example: Climbing those 3.0 m of stairs (2,058 J) in 4.0 s takes 2058/4.0=5152058 / 4.0 = 5152058/4.0=515 W.

26. Power from force and velocity

P=FvP = FvP=Fv

Use it when: a steady force keeps an object moving at constant speed.

Example: A cyclist pushing against 20 N of drag at 10 m/s produces 20×10=20020 \times 10 = 20020×10=200 W.

27. Efficiency

η=useful energy (or power) outtotal energy (or power) in×100%\eta = \frac{\text{useful energy (or power) out}}{\text{total energy (or power) in}} \times 100\%η=total energy (or power) inuseful energy (or power) out​×100%

Use it when: comparing machines. Efficiency is always less than 100% for real devices.

Example: A motor taking 400 W of electrical power and delivering 300 W of mechanical power is 75% efficient.

Rotation

Each linear formula has a rotational partner: mass becomes moment of inertia, force becomes torque (OpenStax University Physics Volume 1, chapters 10–12). Angles must be in radians.

28. Angular velocity and linear speed

ω=ΔθΔt,v=ωr\omega = \frac{\Delta\theta}{\Delta t}, \qquad v = \omega rω=ΔtΔθ​,v=ωr

Symbols: ω\omegaω in rad/s, rrr is radius (m), vvv is the speed of a point at radius rrr (m/s).

Use it when: converting between spinning rate and the speed of a point on the rotating object. One revolution is 2π2\pi2π rad.

Example: A wheel turning at 600 revolutions per minute has ω=600×2π/60=62.8\omega = 600 \times 2\pi / 60 = 62.8ω=600×2π/60=62.8 rad/s. A point on its 0.35 m rim moves at 62.8×0.35=22.062.8 \times 0.35 = 22.062.8×0.35=22.0 m/s.

29. Angular acceleration

α=ΔωΔt,at=αr\alpha = \frac{\Delta\omega}{\Delta t}, \qquad a_t = \alpha rα=ΔtΔω​,at​=αr

Use it when: a spin rate changes. ata_tat​ is the tangential acceleration of a point at radius rrr.

Example: A fan reaching 62.8 rad/s from rest in 4.0 s has α=15.7\alpha = 15.7α=15.7 rad/s². A point 0.30 m from the axis has at=4.71a_t = 4.71at​=4.71 m/s².

30. Torque

τ=rFsin⁡θ\tau = rF\sin\thetaτ=rFsinθ

Symbols: rrr is distance from the pivot to where the force acts (m), θ\thetaθ is the angle between rrr and FFF. Torque is in N·m.

Use it when: working out the turning effect of a force.

Example: A 40 N push at right angles on a spanner 0.25 m long gives τ=0.25×40=10\tau = 0.25 \times 40 = 10τ=0.25×40=10 N·m.

31. Newton's second law for rotation

τnet=Iα\tau_{\text{net}} = I\alphaτnet​=Iα

Use it when: relating net torque to angular acceleration about a fixed axis.

Example: A net torque of 10 N·m on a wheel with I=0.50I = 0.50I=0.50 kg·m² gives α=20\alpha = 20α=20 rad/s².

32. Moment of inertia

I=∑miri2,Isolid disc=12MR2,Ihoop=MR2I = \sum m_i r_i^2, \qquad I_{\text{solid disc}} = \tfrac{1}{2}MR^2, \qquad I_{\text{hoop}} = MR^2I=∑mi​ri2​,Isolid disc​=21​MR2,Ihoop​=MR2

Use it when: finding how hard an object is to spin. Other common shapes: solid sphere 25MR2\tfrac{2}{5}MR^252​MR2, rod about its centre 112ML2\tfrac{1}{12}ML^2121​ML2.

Example: A 2.0 kg solid disc of radius 0.20 m has I=12(2.0)(0.202)=0.040I = \tfrac{1}{2}(2.0)(0.20^2) = 0.040I=21​(2.0)(0.202)=0.040 kg·m².

33. Rotational kinetic energy

KErot=12Iω2KE_{\text{rot}} = \tfrac{1}{2}I\omega^2KErot​=21​Iω2

Use it when: an object spins. A rolling object has both 12mv2\tfrac{1}{2}mv^221​mv2 and 12Iω2\tfrac{1}{2}I\omega^221​Iω2.

Example: The 0.040 kg·m² disc spinning at 50 rad/s stores 12(0.040)(502)=50\tfrac{1}{2}(0.040)(50^2) = 5021​(0.040)(502)=50 J.

34. Angular momentum and its conservation

L=Iω,I1ω1=I2ω2L = I\omega, \qquad I_1\omega_1 = I_2\omega_2L=Iω,I1​ω1​=I2​ω2​

Use it when: no external torque acts, so LLL stays constant.

Example: A skater spinning at 2.0 rad/s with I=3.0I = 3.0I=3.0 kg·m² pulls in their arms to I=1.0I = 1.0I=1.0 kg·m² and spins at ω2=3.0×2.0/1.0=6.0\omega_2 = 3.0 \times 2.0 / 1.0 = 6.0ω2​=3.0×2.0/1.0=6.0 rad/s.

35. Conditions for equilibrium

∑F=0,∑τ=0\sum F = 0, \qquad \sum \tau = 0∑F=0,∑τ=0

Use it when: an object is at rest and not rotating, such as beams, ladders, shelves and seesaws.

Example: A 30 kg child sits 2.0 m from a seesaw's pivot. A 40 kg child balances them at x=30×2.0/40=1.5x = 30 \times 2.0 / 40 = 1.5x=30×2.0/40=1.5 m on the other side.

Gravitation and orbits

Newton's law of gravitation and the motion of satellites (OpenStax University Physics Volume 1, chapter 13). Examples use Earth's mass ME=5.972×1024M_E = 5.972 \times 10^{24}ME​=5.972×1024 kg and mean radius RE=6.371×106R_E = 6.371 \times 10^6RE​=6.371×106 m.

36. Newton's law of universal gravitation

F=Gm1m2r2F = \frac{G m_1 m_2}{r^2}F=r2Gm1​m2​​

Symbols: rrr is the distance between the centres of mass (m).

Use it when: finding the attraction between any two masses.

Example: Earth and the Moon (7.35×10227.35 \times 10^{22}7.35×1022 kg, 3.84×1083.84 \times 10^83.84×108 m apart) attract each other with about 1.98×10201.98 \times 10^{20}1.98×1020 N.

37. Gravitational field strength

g=GMR2g = \frac{GM}{R^2}g=R2GM​

Use it when: finding surface gravity on a planet or ggg at a height above it (use r=R+hr = R + hr=R+h).

Example: For Earth, g=6.674×10−11×5.972×1024/(6.371×106)2=9.82g = 6.674 \times 10^{-11} \times 5.972 \times 10^{24} / (6.371 \times 10^6)^2 = 9.82g=6.674×10−11×5.972×1024/(6.371×106)2=9.82 m/s². The measured value varies from about 9.78 to 9.83 m/s² with latitude and altitude.

38. Orbital speed (circular orbit)

v=GMrv = \sqrt{\frac{GM}{r}}v=rGM​​

Use it when: a satellite is in a circular orbit of radius rrr measured from the planet's centre.

Example: At 400 km altitude, r=6.771×106r = 6.771 \times 10^6r=6.771×106 m and v=7.67v = 7.67v=7.67 km/s, about the speed of the International Space Station.

39. Kepler's third law

T2=4π2GM r3T^2 = \frac{4\pi^2}{GM}\,r^3T2=GM4π2​r3

Use it when: relating an orbit's period to its radius (or semi-major axis for an ellipse).

Example: For the 400 km orbit above, T=2πr3/GM=5545T = 2\pi\sqrt{r^3/GM} = 5545T=2πr3/GM​=5545 s, about 92 minutes.

40. Escape velocity

vesc=2GMRv_{\text{esc}} = \sqrt{\frac{2GM}{R}}vesc​=R2GM​​

Use it when: finding the minimum launch speed to leave a planet with no further thrust, ignoring air resistance.

Example: For Earth, vesc=11.2v_{\text{esc}} = 11.2vesc​=11.2 km/s, exactly 2\sqrt{2}2​ times the orbital speed at the same radius.

41. Gravitational potential energy (general)

U=−GMmrU = -\frac{GMm}{r}U=−rGMm​

Use it when: heights are large compared with the planet's radius. U=0U = 0U=0 at infinite distance, so bound objects have negative energy.

Example: Raising 1 kg from Earth's surface to 400 km takes GM(1/RE−1/r)=3.70×106GM(1/R_E - 1/r) = 3.70 \times 10^6GM(1/RE​−1/r)=3.70×106 J. The approximation mghmghmgh would give 3.93×1063.93 \times 10^63.93×106 J, about 6% too much, because ggg falls with height.

Fluids

Pressure, buoyancy and flow (OpenStax University Physics Volume 1, chapter 14). Fresh water has ρ≈1000\rho \approx 1000ρ≈1000 kg/m³; air at room conditions about 1.2 kg/m³.

42. Density

ρ=mV\rho = \frac{m}{V}ρ=Vm​

Use it when: comparing materials or predicting whether something floats.

Example: A 500 g stone with a volume of 200 cm³ has ρ=2.5\rho = 2.5ρ=2.5 g/cm³, or 2,500 kg/m³.

43. Pressure at depth

P=P0+ρghP = P_0 + \rho g hP=P0​+ρgh

Symbols: P0P_0P0​ is pressure at the surface (Pa), hhh is depth (m).

Use it when: finding pressure in a liquid at rest.

Example: At 10 m in fresh water, the water adds 1000×9.8×10=981000 \times 9.8 \times 10 = 981000×9.8×10=98 kPa. With atmospheric pressure (101 kPa), the total is about 199 kPa, roughly double the surface pressure.

44. Archimedes' principle

Fb=ρfluid Vdisplaced gF_b = \rho_{\text{fluid}}\, V_{\text{displaced}}\, gFb​=ρfluid​Vdisplaced​g

Use it when: finding the upward force on a submerged or floating object. An object floats if it can displace its own weight of fluid.

Example: A fully submerged 0.0020 m³ block in water feels a buoyant force of 1000×0.0020×9.8=19.61000 \times 0.0020 \times 9.8 = 19.61000×0.0020×9.8=19.6 N.

45. Pascal's principle (hydraulics)

F1A1=F2A2\frac{F_1}{A_1} = \frac{F_2}{A_2}A1​F1​​=A2​F2​​

Use it when: a confined fluid transmits pressure between two pistons.

Example: 100 N on a 4.0 cm² piston produces 100×(400/4.0)=10,000100 \times (400 / 4.0) = 10{,}000100×(400/4.0)=10,000 N on a 400 cm² piston, enough to lift about 1,000 kg.

46. Continuity equation

A1v1=A2v2A_1 v_1 = A_2 v_2A1​v1​=A2​v2​

Use it when: an incompressible fluid flows through a pipe that changes width.

Example: Water at 1.0 m/s in a 2.0 cm-diameter hose speeds up to 16 m/s in a 0.50 cm nozzle, because the area is 16 times smaller.

47. Bernoulli's equation

P+12ρv2+ρgh=constantP + \tfrac{1}{2}\rho v^2 + \rho g h = \text{constant}P+21​ρv2+ρgh=constant

Use it when: steady, non-viscous, incompressible flow along a streamline. Faster flow at the same height means lower pressure.

Example: Water speeding up from 2.0 m/s to 4.0 m/s in a horizontal pipe drops in pressure by 12(1000)(42−22)=6000\tfrac{1}{2}(1000)(4^2 - 2^2) = 600021​(1000)(42−22)=6000 Pa.

48. Drag equation

FD=12ρv2CDAF_D = \tfrac{1}{2}\rho v^2 C_D AFD​=21​ρv2CD​A

Symbols: CDC_DCD​ is the drag coefficient (no units), AAA is frontal area (m²).

Use it when: estimating air or water resistance at everyday speeds, where drag grows with v2v^2v2.

λ=hp=hmv\lambda = \frac{h}{p} = \frac{h}{mv}λ=ph​=mvh​

Use it when: finding the wavelength of a moving particle (for speeds well below ccc).

Example: An electron at 1.0×1061.0 \times 10^61.0×106 m/s has λ=6.626×10−34/(9.109×10−31×106)=0.73\lambda = 6.626 \times 10^{-34} / (9.109 \times 10^{-31} \times 10^6) = 0.73λ=6.626×10−34/(9.109×10−31×106)=0.73 nm, comparable to the spacing of atoms in a crystal, which is why electrons diffract off crystals.

99. Mass–energy equivalence

E=mc2E = mc^2E=mc2

Use it when: relating rest mass to energy, for example in nuclear reactions, where the products have slightly less mass than the reactants.

Example: Converting 1.0 g of mass entirely to energy would release 10−3×(3.0×108)2=9.0×101310^{-3} \times (3.0 \times 10^8)^2 = 9.0 \times 10^{13}10−3×(3.0×108)2=9.0×1013 J, about 25 GWh.

How to use physics formulas well

Knowing a formula is only half the job. These habits prevent most lost marks:

  • Convert to SI units first. Kilometres per hour, grams, centimetres and minutes cause more wrong answers than hard physics. Convert to metres, kilograms and seconds before substituting.
  • Check the conditions. The kinematics equations need constant acceleration. The projectile range formula needs equal launch and landing heights. The pendulum formula needs small angles. Ohm's law needs constant resistance.
  • Use kelvins for gases and radiation. PV=nRTPV = nRTPV=nRT, P=εσAT4P = \varepsilon\sigma AT^4P=εσAT4 and Carnot efficiency are wrong with Celsius values.
  • Use radians for rotation. v=ωrv = \omega rv=ωr and at=αra_t = \alpha rat​=αr only work with angles in radians.
  • Check units at the end. If a speed comes out in kg·m, something went wrong. Dimensional analysis catches many algebra slips.
  • Estimate the size. A car's braking distance should be metres, not kilometres. A household current should be a few amps, not thousands.
  • Watch sign conventions. The first law of thermodynamics, the thin lens equation and the Doppler formula all have competing conventions. Use the one your course uses, consistently.
